manual.title: BeSpoke Engine Architecture & Developer Guide
manual.subtitle: The 3x What/How/Why manual and developer guide for the Engine-as-Spine narrative simulation runtime
manual.description: BeSpoke is a bespoke game development language and standalone simulation engine written in pure Zig, designed from the ground up for systemic, emergent, and narrative game simulations. Every component, pipeline, and architectural decision is documented with its behavior (What), mechanism (How), and design intent (Why).

sections.title: Core Architecture & Principles
sections.description: Foundational architectural decisions defining the simulation engine boundary, clock model, and memory layout.

entries.title: Engine-as-Spine Architecture
entries.summary: The simulation VM is main() and owns the master clock, entities, and state, treating graphics engines strictly as peripherals.
entries.synopsis: pub fn main() !void { var world = World.init(...); var vm = VM.init(...); while (running) { vm.step_tick(); bridge.capture_frame(); } }
entries.what: Inverts the traditional game engine model: rather than embedding a scripting language as a guest plugin inside Unity or Godot, BeSpoke is the host spine that owns simulation state, rules, pathfinding, and narrative logic, publishing read-only render frames to peripheral presentation layers.
how: src/main.zig drives the master simulation loop, allocating the World arena and SpatialSystem.
The Virtual Machine steps discrete simulation ticks at a fixed frequency (e.g. 20 Hz or 60 Hz).
DisplayBridge captures double-buffered snapshot frames (RenderFrame) containing entities, waypoints, and dialogue.
Peripheral display renderers (like SDL2 or headless runners) read double-buffered frames and deliver input intents as UserAction events.
entries.why: Scripting embedded in a frame-driven engine tends to inherit frame-rate dependent logic, garbage collection pauses, and coupling to the renderer. Owning the spine keeps the simulation deterministic, testable without a window, and rewindable.

entries.title: Discrete Simulation Tick Clock
entries.summary: Simulation state advances strictly in integer ticks without floating-point delta accumulation.
entries.synopsis: pub fn step_tick(self: *VM) !void { self.world.current_tick += 1; ... }
entries.what: Governs all motor movement, TTL fact expirations, fiber waits, and reactive rule edges using integer tick counters rather than floating-point delta seconds (dt).
how: VM.step_tick() increments World.current_tick by 1 on each discrete simulation step.
Fact TTLs decay by integer ticks and are automatically pruned when current_tick exceeds expires_at_tick.
Fibers suspended via wait_ticks or wait_until wake up when the integer tick target is met.
Visual renderers interpolate fractional positions between consecutive ticks for smooth 60 Hz screen motion.
entries.why: Floating-point delta time introduces accumulation errors, platform-dependent rounding discrepancies, and non-deterministic divergence that destroys replayability and networking. With integer ticks, repeated runs produce identical states; the proof goldens check this on every test run (on Linux x86_64; other platforms are untested).

entries.title: Contiguous Arena Allocation & Zero Raw Pointers
entries.summary: World state is stored in a fixed byte arena with no internal pointers, so a snapshot copies the fact columns as raw bytes.
entries.synopsis: pub const World = struct { arena: std.heap.ArenaAllocator, facts: std.MultiArrayList(Fact), ... }
entries.what: Houses all simulation entities, relations, and fact rows in contiguous array allocations, referencing entities and strings by integer handles rather than raw virtual memory addresses.
how: World initializes an arena allocator with a fixed reserve (e.g. 1 MB).
Facts are stored in Structure-of-Arrays layout via std.MultiArrayList(Fact) with subject, relation, object, and expires_at columns.
Entities are typed 32-bit handles (EntityId) indexing interned string tables.
Serialization (save_state and restore_state) writes and reads raw memory buffers with CRC32 checksums.
entries.why: Raw pointers break across processes, prevent binary snapshot persistence, and cause cache misses during bulk queries. Flat columns keep queries cache-friendly, and a rewind copies the columns back and rebuilds two name maps rather than reconstructing an object graph.

entries.title: Zero External Dependencies Policy
entries.summary: The core simulation runtime, compiler, and VM require zero external C or package dependencies beyond pure Zig.
entries.synopsis: build.zig: exe = b.addExecutable(.{ .name = "bespoke", .root_source_file = b.path("src/main.zig") });
entries.what: The compiler, relational database, bytecode VM, pathfinding, and REPL need only the Zig 0.13 compiler. They are built and tested on Linux x86_64 and wasm32; macOS and Windows builds are written into the template's CI workflow but have never run.
how: The compiler front-end uses custom recursive-descent lexing and Pratt parsing written from scratch.
Display rendering optionally links SDL2 as a peripheral consumer, but falls back seamlessly to headless terminal mode if unavailable.
Documentation tools rely exclusively on the Python 3 standard library.
entries.why: Heavy third-party package dependencies create fragile build pipelines, security supply chain risks, and platform incompatibilities. Zero-dependency design keeps BeSpoke lean, auditable, and easily embeddable.

sections.title: Relational World Database & State
sections.description: The flat 4-tuple relational knowledge graph that drives systemic entity behaviors and world state.

entries.title: Flat 4-Tuple Relational Facts
entries.summary: World state is composed of relational rows: (subject, relation, object, expires_at_tick).
entries.synopsis: pub const Fact = struct { subject: EntityId, relation: RelationId, object: i32, expires_at: u64 };
entries.what: Replaces traditional object-oriented properties and component hierarchies with flat relational fact tuples representing systemic knowledge, inventory possession, spatial co-location, and emotional states.
how: Facts are asserted via World.remember(subject, relation, object, ttl_ticks).
Facts are retracted via World.forget(subject, relation, object).
TTL decay: when ttl_ticks > 0, expires_at is set to current_tick + ttl_ticks.
Pruning: World.prune_expired() scans the facts list at the start of each tick, recording expired rows into a recently_expired ring buffer for expiration hooks.
entries.why: OOP class hierarchies create rigid coupling where adding a new emergent interaction requires modifying multiple classes. Relational facts decouple subjects from attributes, enabling dynamic pattern queries without schema migrations.

entries.title: Functional Single-Value Property Overwrite
entries.summary: Relations marked as functional auto-overwrite previous values on assertion.
entries.synopsis: const carries = try world.intern_relation("Carries", .set); try world.remember(actor, carries, item, 0);
entries.what: Distinguishes between multi-valued relations (e.g. FriendsWith, KnowsSecret) and single-valued functional properties (e.g. Carries, CurrentRoom, Health), automatically retracting old values when a new value is remembered.
how: Relations are registered with RelationKind (.set for functional single-value, .bag for multi-value).
When World.remember is called on a .set relation, World scans for any existing fact matching (subject, relation, _) and overwrites its object and expiry in place.
Ensures an entity cannot simultaneously occupy multiple rooms or hold mutually exclusive single states.
entries.why: Without functional auto-overwrite, script authors would be forced to manually write pair-wise forget statements before every state change, introducing subtle desynchronization bugs when forgetting is overlooked.

entries.title: Multi-Clause Relational Joins & Unification
entries.summary: Evaluates conjunctive fact patterns across active simulation state with backtracking variable unification.
entries.synopsis: when CharmedBy(listener, musician) and Carries(listener, loot):
entries.what: Queries active relational facts using multi-clause patterns joined by 'and', binding wildcard variables (e.g. victim, loot) and returning matching entity tuples.
how: World.find_first_match, has_multi_match, and find_all_matches accept arrays of PatternClause.
Terms can be concrete entities, wildcards, or named variables (PatternTerm.variable).
VariableBindings maintains a scoped mapping of bound entity identifiers.
A backtracking search resolves multi-variable joins across facts in the contiguous MultiArrayList.
entries.why: Systemic games require querying complex social and physical arrangements (e.g. 'Is an alert guard standing in the same room as a distracted thief carrying gold?'). First-class unification eliminates hardcoded conditional checks.

entries.title: CRC32 Snapshots & Time-Travel Rewind
entries.summary: Serialization of the complete world state into a memory buffer, with a CRC32 check on restore.
entries.synopsis: try world.save_state(writer); ... try world.restore_state(reader);
entries.what: Captures the entire relational world state into an in-memory byte buffer on each tick, allowing players and developers to scrub backward or forward across history instantaneously.
how: World.save_state serializes tick count, interned entity names, relations, and fact columns, appending a CRC32 checksum.
World.restore_state verifies the CRC32 checksum, clears the current arena, and restores memory in-place.
DisplayBridge captures a fresh render frame immediately after restore to synchronize peripheral visualization.
When simulation advances after scrubbing into the past, divergent future snapshots are automatically pruned.
entries.why: Debugging systemic simulation bugs requires reproducing non-deterministic edge cases. Snapshot rewind lets developers scrub directly to the tick where a state transition occurred, inspect facts, and test alternative actions.

sections.title: Compiler Pipeline & Bytecode Virtual Machine
sections.description: Source-to-bytecode compilation, stack VM execution, cooperative fibers, and cue dispatching.

entries.title: Bytecode Instruction Set & Stack Machine
entries.summary: Compact stack-based virtual machine executing variable-length bytecode chunks.
entries.synopsis: pub const Opcode = enum(u8) { push_const, remember, forget, wait_ticks, call_routine, emit_cue, halt, ... };
entries.what: Executes compiled BeSpoke programs via a compact bytecode interpreter supporting constants, relational mutations, math, routine calls, cues, and control flow.
how: BytecodeChunk stores an array of byte opcodes and a pool of 32-bit constants.
VM evaluates instructions using an operand stack per fiber.
Relational opcodes (op_remember, op_forget, op_query) operate directly on the World database.
Execution is bounded per tick by max_steps_per_fiber to prevent runaway loops from freezing the engine.
entries.why: Direct AST evaluation has poor cache locality and high tree-walking overhead. A flat bytecode chunk executes in a tight loop and allows serialization of fiber instruction pointers.

entries.title: Cooperative Fiber Scheduler & Temporal Suspension
entries.summary: Fiber-based routine execution suspended across ticks via wait_ticks and wait_until.
entries.synopsis: pub const Fiber = struct { id: FiberId, entity: EntityId, ip: usize, wait_ticks: u32, ... };
entries.what: Executes actor routines concurrently within a single simulation thread using lightweight fibers that yield voluntarily when waiting for time or events.
how: VM maintains an active list of Fiber descriptors, each with its own instruction pointer, call stack, and operand stack.
Instructions like wait_ticks set fiber.wait_ticks, suspending the fiber until the specified tick delay elapses.
wait_until evaluates a relational condition pattern each tick and resumes when satisfied.
On each simulation tick, VM steps all active, non-waiting fibers up to their yield points.
entries.why: Operating system threads introduce non-deterministic race conditions, locks, and heavy memory overhead. Cooperative fibers run in a fixed order on one thread, cost nothing while waiting except their stored state, and serialize cleanly.

entries.title: Recursive-Descent Lexer, Parser & Codegen
entries.summary: Compiles high-level narrative DSL script text directly into bytecode chunks and reactive rule tables.
entries.synopsis: pub fn compile_source(allocator: Allocator, world: *World, spatial: ?*SpatialSystem, source: []const u8) !CompiledProgram
entries.what: Transforms plain-text BeSpoke game scripts into executable bytecode, registering entities, relations, stage marks, hotspots, routines, cue handlers, and reactive when rules.
how: src/compiler/lexer.zig scans source into tokens, handling Python-style indentation (indent/dedent), keywords, and comments.
src/compiler/parser.zig builds an Abstract Syntax Tree (ProgramAst) containing routines, cues, stageplay declarations, and rules.
src/compiler/codegen.zig lowers the AST into BytecodeChunk instructions, populates entry-point lookup tables, and builds CompiledWhenRule arrays.
entries.why: Writing narrative simulations in raw Zig or assembly is tedious for game designers. The BeSpoke DSL provides clean theatrical syntax while compiling to zero-overhead bytecode.

entries.title: Cue Event Dispatch & Priority Interruption
entries.summary: Discrete event cues trigger routine fibers with priority-tiered preemption stacks.
entries.synopsis: vm.fire_cue(compiled, "Uses", actor, target_a, target_b);
entries.what: Delivers external player interactions and systemic world events to registered cue handlers, preempting lower-priority routines and cleanly resuming them upon completion.
how: Cues are emitted via VM.fire_cue, which asks CompiledProgram.select_cue_handler for the most specific matching handler whose where guard holds, with the handler's variable parameters bound to the cue's arguments; a failed guard falls through to the next, less specific handler (D-072).
When an interrupt occurs (e.g. thief alert), the entity's active fiber is pushed onto an interrupt stack.
The higher-priority handler executes to completion.
Opcode resume_routine pops the interrupted fiber state, restoring its instruction pointer and continuing its original routine.
entries.why: Standard event callbacks discard context, forcing actors to restart tasks from scratch after an interruption. Priority stacks let NPCs react urgently to emergencies and then smoothly resume their previous actions.

entries.title: Two-Operand Inventory Combining & Commutative Cues
entries.summary: Supports 3-argument in-hand item combinations with automatic commutative parameter matching.
entries.synopsis: on cue Uses(Player, ItemA, ItemB): ... // Matches ItemA on ItemB and ItemB on ItemA
entries.what: Enables classic adventure game item combining in hand (e.g. using MapleSyrup with CatHairTape) where applying item A to B is functionally identical to applying B to A.
how: Codegen registers composite signature keys: Uses:Actor:ItemA:ItemB and the commutative permutation Uses:Actor:ItemB:ItemA.
CompiledProgram.find_cue_handler checks ternary commutative signatures, falling back to binary and unary forms.
VM.fire_cue resolves entities, matches the handler PC, records an EmittedCue for display peripherals, and spawns the executing routine.
DisplayWindow tracks selected_inventory_item, highlighting the tray item and emitting combine_inventory_items on a second item click.
entries.why: Requiring narrative designers to author two identical script handlers for every combination is error-prone and redundant. Built-in commutativity guarantees symmetric interaction.

sections.title: Spatial System & Navigation
sections.description: 2D topological waypoint graphs, discrete room graphs, A* pathfinding, and screen layout algorithms.

entries.title: Waypoint Node Graphs & Topological Pathfinding
entries.summary: Spatial environments are modeled as discrete 2D waypoint graphs with A* shortest-path routing.
entries.synopsis: pub const WaypointGraph = struct { waypoints: std.ArrayList(Waypoint), edges: std.ArrayList(Edge), ... };
entries.what: Defines rooms and navigable ground locations as integer-coordinate waypoint nodes connected by bidirectional edges, calculating walking paths via discrete A* search.
how: SpatialGraph stores waypoints with room IDs, integer coordinates (x, y), and names.
Edges represent unobstructed walking paths between waypoints.
SpatialGraph.find_path computes the shortest sequence of waypoints using Manhattan/Euclidean integer heuristics.
Actors traverse edges step-by-step at discrete velocities.
entries.why: Continuous 3D physics sandboxes require complex collision meshes and floating-point math that destroy determinism. Topological waypoint graphs fit narrative graphic adventures and keep pathfinding small and deterministic.

entries.title: Asynchronous Motor Intents & Walking
entries.summary: Actor movement is non-blocking and driven by motor intents updated on simulation ticks.
entries.synopsis: spatial.walk_to(actor, target_waypoint_id);
entries.what: Initiates autonomous, asynchronous movement for an agent across the waypoint graph without stalling other fibers or game simulation logic.
how: SpatialSystem.walk_to assigns a target destination and generates a path queue for the agent.
SpatialSystem.update advances agent coordinates toward their next waypoint each tick.
When the final waypoint is reached, agent.is_moving is set to false and arrival events fire.
entries.why: Blocking sleep calls inside entity scripts lock the main thread. Asynchronous motor intents allow actors to navigate while continuously listening for sensory events and dialogue interruptions.

entries.title: Interactive Hotspots & Scene Props
entries.summary: Static interactive objects in the environment with spatial hitboxes, examination text, and verb hooks.
entries.synopsis: spatial.register_hotspot(room, x, y, radius, "Flags", "A pair of starting flags.");
entries.what: Registers interactive scene scenery and props (e.g. Fireplace, Wine Cask, Flags) with radial click hitboxes, examine descriptions, and verb cue triggers.
how: SpatialSystem.register_hotspot interns the hotspot entity and stores its room, coordinates, and radius.
DisplayWindow hit-tests mouse coordinates against active hotspots via hit_test_hotspot.
Clicking a hotspot emits interact_hotspot with the active verb (.look_at, .use_with, .talk_to, .pick_up).
entries.why: Treating scenery as first-class entities allows them to participate in relational facts (e.g. Tampered(Flags, 1)) and reactive when rules alongside living actors.

entries.title: Actor Standoff Separation & Non-Overlapping Labels
entries.summary: Automated 60px horizontal separation, priority-based 2D text layout solver, and standardized scale hierarchy prevent label collision.
entries.synopsis:
pub const TextLayoutResolver = text_layout.TextLayoutResolver;
pub fn get_entity_screen_layout(idx: usize, entities: []const RenderEntity, w: i32, h: i32) EntityScreenLayout
entries.what: Solves the visual crowding problem when multiple actors occupy the exact same waypoint or proximate stage marks by combining actor horizontal standoff spacing with a centralized 2D collision-avoidance label layout engine.
how: get_entity_screen_layout groups entities within 32 pixels into a spatial cluster and spreads them horizontally by ±30px.
TextLayoutResolver collects all floating in-world labels (actor names, status badges, waypoint names, hotspot prompts) and registers actor and waypoint tokens as physical obstacles.
Labels are sorted and placed in descending priority order (hover tooltips = 10, actor alerts = 9, actor names = 8, actor statuses = 7, waypoints = 6/2, props = 1).
Actor names use font scale 2 above tokens; actor status badges use font scale 1 below tokens, cutting width by 50% to establish a clean visual hierarchy.
Contested labels automatically stagger downward across vertical tiers (Tiers 1-3) or flip above, while idle waypoint names yield to preserve legibility without hiding the physical ground mark.
entries.why: In theater and adventure scenes (e.g. Guybrush and Organiser at the Starting Line, or George and Billy Goat at Lochmarne), actors frequently gather at proximate marks. Drawing labels at fixed coordinates produces illegible text overlap. Centralized collision resolution guarantees every string a legible, collision-free slot.

entries.title: Multi-Scene Graph Partitioning & Transitions
entries.summary: Spatial waypoints and props partition by scene while global facts persist across transitions.
entries.synopsis: pub fn transition_actor(self: *SpatialSystem, entity: EntityId, target_room: EntityId, entry_wp: ?WaypointId) !bool
entries.what: Partitions spatial waypoints and interactive hotspots across distinct narrative scenes and rooms, allowing actors to transition between environments via transition to scene statements.
how: Waypoints and hotspots store room EntityIds, scoping navigable nodes and interactables to the active scene.
The compiler AST groups cast, props, and marks under each scene declaration, registering them under the scene entity.
Executing transition to scene updates vm.current_scene, pauses ambient fibers of the previous scene, and wakes target scene fibers.
SpatialSystem.transition_actor relocates actors onto the designated or primary entry waypoint of the new room.
All relational facts in World (inventory, causal puzzle state) persist continuously across scene changes.
entries.why: Destroying world state on room transitions loses cross-scene inventory and puzzle facts, while a single monolithic coordinate space clutters the screen and leaks ambient events across distant rooms. Partitioned spatial graphs with continuous relational facts give clean scene encapsulation with zero serialization overhead.

entries.title: Discrete Grid Overlay
entries.summary: An optional per-room grid whose cell attributes and fire, smoke, and water automata live in World facts.
entries.synopsis: grid <Name> in <Room>:  size W H  cell N  [origin X Y]  flammable|liquid|blocking x y [w h]  place <Mark> x y
entries.what: Overlays a room with a discrete grid of cells carrying flammable, liquid, and blocking attributes, and maps each waypoint to the cell under its position.
how: src/grid.zig defines Grid geometry (room, width, height, cell size, origin); SpatialSystem.grids holds at most one overlay per room.
Each set attribute is a CellFlammable, CellLiquid, or CellBlocking fact on the grid entity whose value is the cell index y*W+x; empty cells have no facts.
A grid script declaration compiles into CompiledProgram.grids; host.initialize_subsystems seeds the layout once and marks it with GridSeeded.
place moves a mark to a cell centre and refreshes its edge costs; SpatialSystem.waypoint_blocked treats a blocking cell like WaypointBlocked for world-aware walks.
.bspk version 7 stores grids; versions 1 through 6 load without them.

Rates burn, spread, dissipate, and flow drive grid.step each host.tick: fires are CellBurning facts whose TTL is their remaining burn, smoke is CellSmoke refreshed by each fire, and liquid floods non-blocking neighbours and douses fire.
All ignitions and floods are decided from the start-of-step state before any applies; agents then carry InBurningCell, InSmokeCell, and InLiquidCell states that when rules react to on the next tick.
entries.why: Fire, flooding, and line-of-sight need area state that a sparse waypoint graph cannot express, while adventure scenes still navigate by waypoints. Keeping cell attributes in World facts lets save, rewind, and temporal branches carry hazard state with no new snapshot channel, and storing only set attributes keeps the fixed-capacity fact table small.

sections.title: Continuous Reactive Simulation Engine
sections.description: Autonomous pattern-matching rule cascades, edge-triggered transitions, and fact expiration hooks in the VM.

entries.title: Continuous When Rule Pattern Matching
entries.summary: Rules are checked against the world's facts on every tick and fire interrupts without any script polling for them.
entries.synopsis: when currently Wind is blowing: loop: animate wind-blowing
entries.what: Provides declarative rule evaluation inside the engine spine: whenever world state matches the rule's relational pattern, the VM triggers associated behavior routines automatically.
how: Codegen compiles when clauses into CompiledWhenRule records with pattern clauses, priority, and entry PC.
VM.evaluate_reactive_rules checks rules on tick boundaries or following fact mutations.
Pattern matches are verified against World using multi-clause relational unification.
entries.why: Polling inside entity scripts creates bloated boilerplate, missed frame events, and CPU thrashing. Built-in reactive evaluation fires a rule on the tick its condition first holds, with no polling code in scripts.

entries.title: Edge-Triggered State Transitions (Rising & Falling)
entries.summary: Fires rule handlers on state boundary transitions (false -> true and true -> false).
entries.synopsis: when Wind stops being blowing: stop animate wind-blowing
entries.what: Distinguishes between continuous state and transitional edges, firing rising-edge handlers on positive transition and falling-edge handlers on negative transition without repeated triggers.
how: ReactiveRule tracks was_active from the preceding tick.
Rising edge fires when was_active is false and the pattern match becomes true.
Falling edge (when X stops being Y) fires when was_active was true and the condition becomes false.
Re-arming occurs automatically once the condition clears.
entries.why: Continuous level-triggered rules would re-execute every tick while a condition remains true, spawning runaway fibers. Edge-triggering ensures handlers fire exactly once per state transition.

entries.title: TTL Fact Expiration Hooks (when forgets)
entries.summary: Fires reactive routines when temporary timed facts expire naturally from the world database.
entries.synopsis: when Organiser forgets Distracted: walk Organiser to Starting Line
entries.what: Allows scripts to react to the natural decay of temporary facts (e.g. distraction timers, charmed status, temporary alerts) without requiring manual bookkeeping or timers.
how: When World.prune_expired removes a fact whose TTL has elapsed, it copies the row into a recently_expired buffer.
VM evaluates on_expire reactive rules against recently_expired during the tick step.
Matches trigger interrupt routines (e.g. Organiser walks back to the starting line after crowd distraction ends).
entries.why: Manual timer countdown routines in scripts are error-prone and hard to synchronize with world state. Integrating expiration into the fact store means an expiry and its rule fire on the same tick every run.

entries.title: Arrival Rules (when arrives at)
entries.summary: Fires a reactive routine when an actor completes a walk at a named mark.
entries.synopsis: when George arrives at DigOpening: transition to scene: Templar Crypt
entries.what: Lets a script react to an actor reaching a mark, so rules such as a guard animal charging whoever reaches a doorway live in the script and not in host code. The rule fires once per completed walk. Resting on the mark, walking through it toward another mark, and being placed there by the host do not fire it.
how: The parser reads when <Actor> arrives at <Mark>: and rejects an undeclared mark or a missing 'at' with line and column.
Codegen emits a reactive rule with the on_arrive edge and one clause holding the actor and the mark's waypoint id.
MotorAgent raises arrival_pending when a walk intent completes, including a walk to the mark the actor already stands on.
VM.evaluate_reactive_rules checks arrival rules after the motor steps in the same tick, interrupts the actor's routine (or spawns one), then clears every pending arrival.
entries.why: A host loop that polls an actor's waypoint each tick is a level check: it re-fires while the actor stands still and keeps game rules outside the script. An edge fired inside the tick needs no host dispatch, so every host gets the same behaviour.

entries.title: Priority Rule Cascades & Preemption
entries.summary: Rules with higher priority preempt lower-priority routines and restore them upon completion.
entries.synopsis: active_priority: u8, interrupt_entity_priority: [16]u8
entries.what: Enforces behavioral priority hierarchies among reactive rules (e.g. theft alarms supersede charming melodies, which supersede idle wandering).
how: Each CompiledWhenRule carries a priority value (default 0, higher numbers indicate greater urgency).
VM checks if rule.priority > vm.active_priority before interrupting an entity.
The active fiber is pushed onto an interrupt stack.
When the high-priority routine completes, the VM pops the previous routine and continues execution.
entries.why: Without priority stacks, any incidental event could permanently overwrite a critical reaction (such as a guard failing to raise an alarm because an idle bard started playing a song).

entries.title: State Inspector: Facts, Dialogue, and Deadlines
entries.summary: A paused view of relational state, dialogue availability and pruning reasons, and the next fact deadlines.
entries.synopsis: [P] then [Tab] to STATE; arrows, Enter, Backspace, Home, F
entries.what: Draws the selected entity and its relationships, lists values and states, explains which dialogue branches are active or pruned, and orders upcoming fact expirations.
how: DisplayBridge.capture_frame copies up to 128 facts per frame with subject and object ids, whether the object names an entity, and the facts that just expired.
state_graph.default_focus picks the entity with most edges; state_graph.build places it in the centre and its neighbours on a ring in entity-id order.
Facts whose object is an entity are arrows; Believes, Knows, and Rejects arrows are purple; value and state facts are listed beside the graph.
Colours: white permanent, then green, amber, and red as fewer than 60 and 20 ticks remain, grey for just expired.

Newly compiled choice blocks write source-order DialogueBranch facts. Active branches are green; pruned branches are red and show the first guard that failed. Generated and older sets show their offered choices as active.
state_graph.next_expiring sorts the next six captured live TTL deadlines by expiration tick and stable fact identity; it does not execute future ticks.
The inspector is the third tab of the P drawer, so the game is paused; Enter, digits, and Space never save or load there.

Left and Right select a ring node; Enter or a click centres on it, Backspace returns through up to eight earlier centres, and Home resets. F cycles the filter: all, beliefs, then each relation in the frame. Navigation is window state and never enters a save.
entries.why: A text list cannot show how state connects or why a conversation option disappeared. Persisting branch diagnostics as World facts keeps the explanation correct after save, rewind, and temporal restore; projecting only known deadlines keeps the inspector read-only and deterministic.

entries.title: Typed Commands: Words, Frames, and Nouns
entries.summary: The vocabulary that turns a typed line into a cue and the entities it names.
entries.synopsis: command <Cue>: "verb <thing> prep <thing>"   alias <Entity>: "phrase", "phrase"
entries.what: Lets players type commands such as pour grog into mug: input becomes words, a frame names the cue, and each noun resolves to an entity the actor can see or holds.
how: command.tokenize lowercases input and drops punctuation and the articles a, an, the; prepositions such as with, into, and about are kept.
A frame is lowercase words with up to two <thing> slots; the engine provides frames for LooksAt, Uses, TalksTo, and WalksTo, and script command lines add more.
An entity's name splits into words at capitals and separators, and alias lines add words; a noun matches when all its words belong to the entity.
Scope.gather collects agents, hotspots, and marks in the actor's room plus what it Carries or holds InInventory; resolve reports one match, several, or none.
.bspk version 10 stores command and alias declarations.
command.Interpreter matches script frames before the defaults, resolves each slot in scope, and keeps one open Which do you mean question that a following bare noun answers.
host.run_command fires the matched cue, walks for WalksTo, and returns a reply when a word is unknown, a sentence or noun does not fit, or no handler answers (Nothing happens).

DisplayWindow.enable_command_bar shows a bar above the verb row: Enter focuses it, every key is then text, Esc leaves, Up and Down recall history, and Tab completes from host.command_words; submitted lines arrive as UserAction.typed_command.
entries.why: Proofs name their own cues, so typed commands need script-owned verbs on top of a few shared defaults. Resolving nouns only in scope keeps typed commands from reaching what the player cannot see, and refusing to guess between two matches keeps the parser predictable.
