entries.title: Agendas: Proactive Social Agency
entries.summary: Script-declared intentions that set an NPC pursuing a target when facts hold or are missing.
entries.synopsis: agenda <Name>:  actor A  target T  [priority N]  [cooldown N]  [once]  requires Rel(A, B)  unless Rel(A, B)
entries.what: Lets an NPC react to what the player did, or failed to do, by starting to pursue them; the engine chooses which agendas pursue and keeps their stages as facts.
how: An agenda declaration compiles into CompiledProgram.agendas; requires lines must hold, unless lines must not, with names or _ wildcards.
Each agenda entity carries AgendaState(Agenda, Idle | Pursuing | Done); cooldowns are AgendaCooldown facts that expire after N ticks.

agency.step runs in host.tick: a pursuing agenda whose trigger lapses returns to Idle, and for each target one triggered agenda starts pursuing, chosen by priority, then route cost, then declaration order.
agency.resolve ends a pursuit: once agendas become Done, others return to Idle with their cooldown.
.bspk version 9 stores agendas.

agency.pursue walks each pursuer to its target's last waypoint, re-planning when the target reaches a new one; once both stand idle on one waypoint the agenda resolves and host.tick fires Intercepts(Actor, Target, Agenda).
A Pursuing(Actor) fact holds while an actor pursues, and Society routines do not move an actor that holds it.
entries.why: Wandering characters on fixed schedules only answer when asked. Agendas let them act on player behaviour, including omissions, while every stage stays in the fact store so saves, rewinds, and branches carry it, and constant trigger lines avoid changing the reactive rule engine.

sections.title: Narrative DSL & Adventure UI
sections.description: High-level theater declarations, natural language state transitions, verb interfaces, and dialogue trees.

entries.title: Declarative Stageplay Syntax & Taxonomy
entries.summary: Theater-like script headers declaring scenes, cast, props, marks, and natural state assertions.
entries.synopsis: scene: Booty Island; cast: Guybrush, Organiser; props: Flags; marks: Starting Line
entries.what: Allows authors to declare game environments using natural stageplay vocabulary (scene, cast, props, marks) and transition states using readable sentences (now Flags are tampered with).
how: Parser registers cast members as actor agents, props as hotspots, and marks as spatial waypoints automatically.
State declarations ('now X is Y' and 'now X is not Y') are lowered directly into World.remember and World.forget operations.
Natural state queries ('if Flags are Tampered With:') compile to relational database queries.
entries.why: Requiring narrative designers to write low-level registration functions and numeric IDs causes cognitive friction and high bug rates. Natural stageplay syntax reads like a screenplay while compiling to fast bytecode.

entries.title: Stageplay Paths & Route Pruning
entries.summary: Named operational approaches own fact assertions and guarded routines; PathActive prunes dialogue and WaypointBlocked facts lock spatial waypoints.
entries.synopsis: path Wits: remember WaypointBlocked(BackAlley)  |  VM.select_path(compiled, "Wits")
entries.what: Adds top-level path blocks for mutually exclusive narrative approaches. A path owns its initial fact statements and routines, and only the selected route can run them. A path can also lock waypoints, assert obstacle facts that feed portal access, and prune rival dialogue repertoires.
how: The parser accepts `path Name:` blocks containing `remember`, `forget`, and `now` statements plus nested routines.
`VM.select_path` asserts `PathActive(Name)` in World facts and spawns the reserved `#path:<Name>` initializer, which runs on the next tick.
Every path-owned routine starts with a `PathActive(Name)` guard and halts before its body when another route is active.
`WaypointBlocked(Mark)` facts are read by `SpatialSystem.walk_to_with_world`, which asks A* to exclude each locked waypoint when a scripted walk is planned.

Path initializers can assert existing obstacle predicates such as `Trapped` or `PortalBlocked`; `can_access_portal` reads current World facts. `choice ... if PathActive(Name)` prunes route-specific dialogue.
The existing `.bspk` routine and relation tables carry path initializers without a format bump; save and rewind restore the selected route and its topology effects as ordinary facts.
entries.why: Operational approaches in multi-path adventures must prune incompatible puzzle branches without host-language flags. Keeping the route, waypoint locks, and obstacle facts in World facts preserves determinism, saves, and rewind; routine-local guards mute alternatives even when a host spawns them directly.

entries.title: Three-Path Algiers Bazaar & Route Selector
entries.summary: A generated selector chooses Wits, Fists, or Team; each path locks the rival gates, prunes Omar's dialogue, and runs only its own solution.
entries.synopsis: path Wits: remember WaypointBlocked(FistsGate)  |  VM.select_path(compiled, "Wits")  |  --atlantis
entries.what: The Algiers Bazaar proof stages Omar's bazaar as one spatial graph with three gates. The selected path asserts WaypointBlocked facts on the two rival gates, so the same walk plans through the chosen approach, and PathActive guards reduce Omar's dialogue to the matching clue plus a neutral exit.
how: The script declares `path Wits`, `path Fists`, and `path Team`, each with route facts and a `Solve...` routine.
A generated dialogue opens three selector options in the native window; clicking one or pressing `1` to `3` calls `VM.select_path`.
The path initializer runs on the next tick, locks the rival gates, and records `Chosen(Indy, <Path>)`.
Scripted walks call `SpatialSystem.walk_to_with_world`, so A* plans around the locked gates and reaches `ManuscriptMark` through the open route.
`Talk` offers only the selected path's choice plus the neutral exit, and `[S]` runs only that path's solution routine.
entries.why: Multi-path adventures need one topology and one dialogue source that reshape themselves around an operational choice. Keeping the choice, gate locks, and obstacle facts in World facts means saves, rewinds, and snapshots carry the whole route without a host-side branch table.

entries.title: Classic 5-Verb Interaction Bar
entries.summary: Five classic adventure verbs: WALK, LOOK, TALK, TAKE, USE with active button highlight and right-click cycling.
entries.synopsis: pub const AdventureVerb = enum(u8) { walk = 0, look_at = 1, talk_to = 2, pick_up = 3, use_with = 4 };
entries.what: Implements the foundational SCUMM-inspired adventure interface: players choose a verb via the bottom HUD bar or right-click cycling, then click objects, actors, or waypoints in the scene.
how: DisplayWindow renders verb buttons in the bottom HUD bar, highlighting the active verb in amber gold.
Right-click cycles active_verb through the enumeration.
Left-click evaluates hit testing: waypoints trigger walk_player, actors trigger interact_actor, and hotspots trigger interact_hotspot.
entries.why: Direct point-and-click single-verb interfaces lack expressiveness. The 5-verb system empowers players to inspect, converse, take, and use objects systemically.

entries.title: Branching Dialogue Trees & Dynamic Choice Pruning
entries.summary: A wrapped dialogue panel with the speaker's name, the line, and relational fact-guarded choices that suspend the script until selection.
entries.synopsis: choice "Rent motorcycle" if Carries(Gabriel, License): say Buthane: "Keys."
entries.what: Shows the open dialogue in a parchment panel along the bottom of the stage: the speaker's display name, the line word-wrapped, and numbered choices that wrap and grow the panel upward, with scrolling past six and keyboard hotkeys (1-9). The window and the browser draw the same layout (D-077).
how: dialogue_panel.layout wraps the speaker, prompt, and choices into rows for a panel width and font scale, and reports each choice's vertical span; it has no SDL dependency, so the desktop renderer and the wasm canvas share it.
dialogue_panel.display_name splits CamelCase entity names for display (BosunPike reads Bosun Pike).
Fibers executing choice blocks evaluate relational guards, record the eligible options as World facts, and suspend until a selection resumes the chosen body.
The renderer displays numbered hotkey labels [1] through [9] and supports mouse clicks on any row of a choice, mouse wheel scrolling, and number keys 1-9; the browser answers clicks and number keys.
The open set lives in World facts, so snapshots and rewinds carry it; RenderFrame.dialogue publishes it to the balloon by revision.
Dismissing a balloon or choosing an option emits dialogue_choice or dismiss_dialogue user actions.

A host can queue click-through messages (queue_message, D-080): each shows alone in the panel's place with a continue hint, a click, Enter, or Space dismisses it, and the choices beneath stay hidden and unanswerable until all are read.
entries.why: Hardcoding dialogue choices in host language ladders causes script fragmentation and breaks time-travel rewinds. Fact-guarded choice trees declared in DSL prune systemically based on active inventory and knowledge facts.

entries.title: In-Hand Tray Selection & Crafting UX
entries.summary: Two-step inventory click flow with golden highlight, in-hand status prompts, and combining feedback.
entries.synopsis: selected_inventory_item: ?usize = null; UserAction.combine_inventory_items
entries.what: Provides an intuitive point-and-click inventory crafting experience: clicking an item selects it into hand, displaying a golden glow, while subsequent clicks apply it to scene targets or combine it with another inventory item.
how: Clicking an inventory item sets selected_inventory_item and switches verb to USE, displaying '[IN HAND: Item]' and banner prompts.
The selected item renders with an amber background (rgb 85, 65, 25) and a glowing golden double border (rgb 250, 204, 21).
Clicking a different item emits combine_inventory_items.
Clicking an actor emits use_inventory_on_actor; clicking a hotspot emits use_inventory_on_hotspot.
Right-click cancels in-hand mode with an 'Action cancelled' banner.
entries.why: Classic multi-step puzzles (like the GK3 Cat Moustache) require crafting composite items before using them in the world. Visual in-hand indicators make the player's intent crystal clear.

entries.title: The Gabriel Knight 3 Cat Moustache Scenario
entries.summary: Multi-scene vertical slice demonstrating ambient routines, in-hand crafting, fact-guarded dialogue pruning, and disguise evaluation.
entries.synopsis: zig build run-proof -- --gk3 [--headless]
entries.what: Implements the classic multi-step disguise puzzle across three partitioned scenes (Hotel Corridor, Courtyard Garden, Bike Rental Desk), combining stolen passport, tape fence traps, spray bottles, syrup adhesive, and fact-guarded dialogue choice validation.
how: Declares three partitioned scenes with distinct waypoints, marks, hotspots, and ambient actor routines.
Uses two-operand inventory combining (Uses(Gabriel, Syrup, CatHair)) to craft composite items.
Evaluates composite disguise validity via relational fact conjunctions (passport, hair, syrup, marker).
Runs dialogue choice pruning when interacting with Madame Buthane, granting motorcycle keys only when the disguise condition holds.
entries.why: Proves that BeSpoke's engine spine effortlessly coordinates complex adventure game logic across multiple scenes, ambient actor schedules, dynamic fact guards, and time-travel snapshot state without custom ad-hoc engine extensions.

entries.title: The Broken Sword Lochmarne Goat Scenario
entries.summary: Authentic 1996 threat-radius reactive interrupt, 30-tick retreat recovery window, plough obstacle dragging, and subterranean crypt multi-scene transition.
entries.synopsis: zig build run-proof -- --goat [--headless]
entries.what: Implements the famous 1996 Lochmarne Castle courtyard puzzle, modeling goat proximity charging, knockback interrupts, dynamic 30-tick retreat recovery windows, plough dragging to trap the tether rope, and subterranean Templar excavation crypt transitions.
how: Approaching Peagram's cellar pit triggers the goat's proximity charge cue, knocking George back and asserting a 30-tick GoatRetreating fact.
Interacting with the heavy farm plough during the retreat window hauls it into the rope line, tangling the goat and clearing the pit.
Descending the excavation ladder transitions simulation state from the Lochmarne Castle ruins courtyard into the subterranean Templar crypt.
Renders authentic Irish courtyard ruins with dynamic rope lines, Celtic whistle audio, and Templar altar reliefs.
entries.why: Demonstrates that BeSpoke's relational fact engine and fiber scheduler solve notoriously frustrating timing puzzles deterministically with discrete ticks, eliminating real-time frame rate dependencies while preserving authentic narrative pacing.

entries.title: Day of the Tentacle Multi-Character Temporal Scenario
entries.summary: Multi-character party switching, generalized inventory transfers across actors, epistemic dialogue belief pruning, and DAG temporal causality cascades across 400 years.
entries.synopsis: zig build run-proof -- --dott [--headless]
entries.what: Implements the three-era Day of the Tentacle puzzle milestone across 1790 Colonial, 1993 Motel, and 2193 Future scenes with three coordinated protagonists (Hoagie, Bernard, Laverne).
how: Tracks party coordination via party array and active_character, rendering top HUD character portrait buttons for instant protagonist switching.
Executes generalized inventory item transfer (World.transfer_item) via atomic relational swaps, enforcing matter conservation without pointer manipulation.
Evaluates NPC dialogue options through epistemic belief facts (Believes, Knows, Rejects), pruning Persuade choices dynamically until supporting evidence is established.

Enforces strict past-to-future DAG causality cascades where past physical modifications (painting trees, sealing wine in time capsules, altering flag designs) instantaneously project forward across present and future eras.
entries.why: Demonstrates that BeSpoke's relational fact engine, fiber scheduler, and discrete tick clock natively support non-linear multi-protagonist agency and historical causality without paradoxical state duplication or ad-hoc temporal flags.

evidence.label: Day of the Tentacle Puzzle Scenario

entries.title: Branch Worlds (Temporal Hypervisor) & Path Previews
entries.summary: A temporary copy of the world that runs on a countdown and either merges back or is discarded, plus precomputed path lines drawn ahead of an actor.
entries.synopsis: zig build run-proof -- --darko [--headless]
entries.what: TemporalHypervisor forks the primary World into a temporary branch world with a countdown. The branch merges back when its closure condition holds, or is discarded when the countdown runs out. The Middlesex Anomaly proof uses it for a time-loop puzzle.
how: fork_branch copies the primary World with World.clone() and starts a countdown of collapse_budget_ticks.
Each step_tick advances the branch one tick and runs check_loop_closure: the keystone entity must stand on the convergence waypoint and a ConvergenceReady, VortexReady, or LoopClosed fact must hold.

On closure, collapse_branch commits the keystone and any recorded residue facts to the primary World (resolved_and_merged). If the countdown runs out first, the branch is discarded (budget_expired) and the player rewinds.
SpatialSystem.get_agent_vector_conduit precomputes an actor's A* route as a polyline that the renderer draws as a preview line.
VM.spawn_hyper_temporal_routine starts a routine at priority 255 so a guide character's lines cannot be preempted.

Hosts register cause-to-effect edges between relations with register_teleological_dependency. is_teleologically_justified follows them (a bounded search, so a cycle terminates), and is_novikov_consistent rejects an action that the edges lead to a paradox, or any action while the actor holds the paradox (D-073).
entries.why: A branch that is a full World copy needs no special rules for which facts it may touch: everything inside it is ordinary facts, and save, rewind, and the inspector treat it like the primary World (D-048, D-049). D-044 gives the mechanism neutral names so other games can use it.

entries.title: Musical Drafts and The Bell Tower Scenario
entries.summary: Four-note pitch drafts declared in the DSL, played on a distaff, reversed for complementary effects, and dispatched through Weave cues.
entries.synopsis: draft Kindle(C, D, E, C) reverse Douse  |  weave Kindle on Beacon  |  zig build run-proof -- --loom [--headless]
entries.what: Adds pitch-based spellcraft: `draft` declarations name four-note sequences over C to B, `weave` statements and player note input cast them on targets, and the original Bell Tower slice teaches drafts by observation and gates the high notes behind the distaff's reach.
how: The parser rejects malformed drafts and any sequence that matches another draft forward or reversed, so a played phrase names at most one draft; a declared reverse becomes its own table entry.

VM.weave_notes resolves played notes and runs the exact Weave(caster, draft, target) handler, or records a WeaveFizzled cue; in-script weaves queue until the host calls dispatch_pending_weaves after each tick.

DistaffInput holds the phrase in progress and the reach limit host-side, never in the world arena; the display bridge copies it into RenderFrame.distaff for the staff HUD, and notes sound through AudioEvent.play_note.
The Bell Tower requires reversing a taught draft (Bind into Loose), extends reach with the tuning fork, and lights the beacon from inside the Toll handler through host re-dispatch.
entries.why: Drafts reuse the verb-as-cue path and the relational store instead of adding a parallel spell system, so effects stay scriptable, rewindable, and testable headless.

entries.title: Container Degradation and The Caustic Grog Sprint
entries.summary: Script-declared vessels lose volume through movement spill and advance through ordered TTL damage stages to a terminal failure location, while atomic pours conserve every remaining measure.
entries.synopsis: degradation CausticGrogCups: stage GrogSound 4 ... vessel CupA 10 10 GrogSound  |  spill 1  |  zig build run-proof -- --grog [--headless]
entries.what: Adds fact-backed container lifecycles: a top-level `degradation` declaration names a substance, ordered damage stages with exposure durations, vessels with capacities and starting stages, and a per-tick spill rate. The original Caustic Grog sprint carries corrosive grog from a dockside barrel to a prison lock before three cups dissolve.
how: `ContainerSystem.init` validates the declaration, interns its fact vocabulary, and seeds each vessel's stage, volume, and exposure deadline as World facts; `host.tick` advances the lifecycle automatically.
`ContainerSystem.pour` moves the source's whole volume into one empty compatible vessel or changes nothing. Damage stays with each vessel and only the destination's exposure deadline restarts.
Moving spill follows `Carries(holder, vessel)` and the holder's motor state; a vessel that reaches its terminal stage empties and records its holder's waypoint as the failure location.

The proof demonstrates terminal failure before the sprint, a rewind to the pristine opening, a full World/Spatial/VM save round-trip, two exact pours, transit spill, and delivery of at least four measures to the lock.
The showcase site's seventh browser deck stages the same three cups with a deck-owned after-tick rule, so the mechanic is playable without compiling a script into the wasm module.
entries.why: Container decay belongs to the same relational spine as every other mechanic: stage, volume, deadline, and failure location are facts, so snapshots, rewinds, and saves carry the whole cascade without subsystem-specific state.

entries.title: Script Scores: MML Music and Its Triggers
entries.summary: Scripts compose four-part chiptune music in Music Macro Language and choose it by scene or by narrative event.
entries.synopsis: score Calm: (lead, bass, chords, drums, scene lines) | play score Chase | stop score
entries.what: A score declares lead, bass, chords, and drums parts in MML, optionally bound to scenes. play score and stop score override scene music from any routine, cue, or rule. The synthesizer plays the four parts in step and loops them together.
how: mml.parse turns each part's text into integer-timed events at 192 ticks per whole note: notes, rests, k/s/h drum hits, tempo, volume, and envelope presets, with ties, re-read [ ]n repeats, and one L loop point. Errors report the script line and column.
The synthesizer runs one integer tick clock for all four parts; a tempo in any part sets it for all. When every part has ended, each part with an L restarts there on the same tick.
@0 sounds like the engine's grid music; @1 to @7 are organ, pluck, long fade, swell, staccato, tremolo, and soft pad, released at each note's written length. v0 to v15 scale volume.

scene lines seed SceneScore(Scene, Score) facts; play score sets the PlayingScore property of Music and stop score removes it. The frame resolves the override, else the scene default, to current_score.

host.ScriptSoundtrack turns a program's scores into a soundtrack whose tracks are named after them; the audio bridge plays the track whose name the frame gives. bespoke run registers it and, headless, prints each change of music.
Packages (version 11) store the MML text and re-parse it on load.
entries.why: Music that follows the story belongs in the script, beside the scenes and rules that cause it. Keeping the choice in World facts makes save, rewind, and temporal branches restore the music with everything else, and integer time keeps four parts from drifting.

sections.title: Authoring Games
sections.description: Starting a project, writing scenes, dialogue, and reactive puzzles, and driving the engine from a Zig host.

entries.title: Authoring Guide: Scenes, Dialogue, and Reactive Puzzles
entries.summary: docs/AUTHORING.md teaches a game author the script language through three walkthroughs whose scripts the test suite compiles and plays.
entries.synopsis: docs/AUTHORING.md | <!-- example: scene|dialogue|puzzle --> | zig build test
entries.what: The guide starts from bespoke init, explains entities, facts, routines, cues, and rules, then builds a two-scene quay, a conversation whose options depend on facts, and a timed lantern-and-bell puzzle. It ends with testing, the host API, and known limits.
how: Every bespoke-fenced block in the guide is a whole script. src/authoring_guide_test.zig reads the guide, compiles each block in a fresh World, and reports a failure by guide line and script position.

The three walkthroughs are found by their example markers and played headless: the test types commands with host.run_command, answers choices with VM.choose, and checks the facts, speech, scene, and music the guide describes.
The build declares docs/AUTHORING.md as an input of the test run, so an edit to the guide re-runs the tests instead of reusing a cached pass.

The stock runner supports the walkthroughs end to end: the window answers dialogue clicks and number keys and enables the command bar for the first routine's actor; a headless run prints speech, scene changes, and offered choices.
entries.why: Examples drift when nothing runs them. Compiling and playing the guide's own text makes a stale example a test failure, and wiring the stock runner means the guide's instructions work in the program every new project starts from.

entries.title: Starter Template: Bundled Releases, Browser Builds, and CI
entries.summary: bespoke init writes a project that tests, builds a self-contained release, builds a browser version, and carries a CI workflow for Linux, macOS, Windows, and the web.
entries.synopsis: zig build test | zig build -Dbundle -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe | zig build web | node web/smoke.js | zig build test-template
entries.what: The generated project's build compiles the script with the engine's own compiler for releases and for the browser, embeds the package, and runs it through the stock runner or the wasm runtime. A GitHub Actions workflow repeats the build and tests on three operating systems and checks the browser build.
how: -Dbundle runs the engine's bespoke compile, built for the build machine, on scripts/main.bespoke and embeds the .bspk as game_package; src/main.zig passes it to bespoke.run_bytes.
zig build web builds src/web.zig for wasm32-freestanding against the engine module (no libc or SDL there) with the same package, and installs it with web/index.html into zig-out/web/.
wasm.script_deck loads the package, starts it with host.start_script, ticks through host.tick, shows speech and choices in the banner, and lets the number keys answer an open dialogue.

The workflow fetches the engine at BESPOKE_ENGINE_REF beside the game, rewrites .path in build.zig.zon, installs SDL2 per platform, tests, builds and runs the bundled release headless, and smoke-tests the browser build with Node.
zig build test-template in the engine generates a project into the cache and runs its tests, bundled build, and web build.
entries.why: A starter that only builds on the author's machine teaches the wrong habit. Compiling the script at build time catches script errors before release and gives one file to ship, and running the same package in the browser keeps the web version in step with the native one.

entries.title: Host Kit API: Driving the Engine from Zig
entries.summary: A host compiles a script, ticks it through host.tick, reads speech after each tick, and routes typed commands and dialogue choices to the VM.
entries.synopsis: compile_source | host.initialize_subsystems | host.run_initial_statements | host.place_cast | host.tick | host.run_command | VM.choose | host.Session
entries.what: The bespoke module exports the calls every game host needs: compilation and checking, package loading, the lifecycle tick, speech collection, typed-command dispatch, dialogue views and answers, path selection, the interactive Session loop, and the script soundtrack.
how: compile_source interns a script's entities and marks into a World and SpatialSystem; host.initialize_subsystems seeds declared grids, agendas, and containers and is safe to repeat.
host.tick runs one lifecycle tick: the VM, containers, grids, agendas, and queued weaves. Hosts never call VM.step_tick alone, or declared rules do not run.
Speech is read after every tick with host.speech_this_tick or SpeechLog, because the next tick clears the emitted cues.
host.run_command interprets a typed line for an actor and fires its cue; dialogue.view and VM.choose present and answer the open set of choices.

host.start_script runs the top-level statements, places the cast, starts every routine, and returns the player; the stock runner, the guide test, and browser script decks all start scripts this way (D-066).
host.place_cast puts each cast member on the first mark of its scene unless the host already placed it (D-065); call it before starting routines.
host.Session owns the timeline, rewind, scrub, saves, pause, and single step for a window host.
entries.why: Hosts that copied loop and speech plumbing drifted apart. One documented kit keeps every host on the same lifecycle, and the authoring guide's table gives authors the contract without reading engine source.

sections.title: Developer Tooling & Diagnostics
sections.description: Interactive developer inspection HUD, time-travel timeline scrubber, live REPL console, and CLI runners.

entries.title: In-Engine Relational Fact & Fiber HUD
entries.summary: Live developer dashboard overlay displaying active facts, TTL counters, fibers, call stacks, and spatial coordinates.
entries.synopsis: Toggle via [F1] or [D] key in running interactive window
entries.what: Provides a HUD overlay drawn directly in the running game window to inspect the live simulation spine.
how: DisplayWindow.render_frame inspects RenderFrame debug fields when show_debug_overlay is true.
Lists all active relational facts with remaining TTL ticks.
Displays active fiber IDs, program counters, priority levels, and call stacks.
Displays agent spatial coordinates, waypoints, and transit statuses.
entries.why: Attaching external debuggers (gdb/lldb) halts execution and cannot display high-level domain concepts like relational facts, TTLs, or fibers. An in-engine HUD gives instant visibility at 60 Hz.

entries.title: Interactive Timeline Scrubber & Replay
entries.summary: Graphical timeline scrubber bar allowing point-and-click time-travel scrubbing across simulation history.
entries.synopsis: Click timeline bar or use [<] / [>] keys to scrub ticks live
entries.what: Enables developers and players to pause time, scrub backward across recorded historical ticks, inspect the world at any previous tick, and resume from the past.
how: The top HUD bar renders a full-width timeline scrubber indicating current tick and max recorded tick.
Left-clicking anywhere on the bar computes target tick from horizontal mouse position and emits scrub_to_tick.
Keyboard left/right arrow keys step single ticks backward and forward.
World.restore_state unpacks the snapshot into memory, and DisplayBridge refreshes the frame.
If the simulation steps forward after scrubbing backward, divergent future history is cleanly truncated.
entries.why: Diagnosing why an NPC took an action 50 ticks ago normally requires restarting the game and adding print statements. The timeline scrubber turns time into a navigable spatial axis.

entries.title: Live Interactive REPL Console Drawer
entries.summary: In-engine slide-out console drawer executing live simulation commands without pausing or recompiling.
entries.synopsis: Toggle via [Tab], [C], or [`]; commands: remember, forget, cue, walk, facts, step, help
entries.what: Provides an interactive command drawer inside the running simulation to query facts, inject new relations, emit cues, or move actors on the fly.
how: src/repl.zig implements a pure Zig command interpreter (Repl) with zero GUI dependencies.
DisplayWindow captures keyboard text input via SDL_TEXTINPUT when show_console is active.
Commands modify World, SpatialSystem, and VM directly and log output to the console history buffer.
entries.why: Testing whether a puzzle reacts to a specific fact requires either playing through prerequisites or recompiling. The live REPL allows instant hypothesis testing in a live simulation.

entries.title: Dual Interactive & Headless CLI Modes
entries.summary: Command-line flags supporting headless deterministic simulation runs and interactive graphics mode.
entries.synopsis: zig build run -- [--headless] [--spitting-contest] [--gk3] [--help]
entries.what: Provides flexible command-line execution modes for CI pipelines, automated integration testing, and interactive human gameplay.
how: --headless runs the simulation without creating an SDL2 window, printing tick snapshots to standard output.
--spitting-contest launches the Monkey Island 2 Booty Island Spitting Contest puzzle scenario.
--gk3 or --cat-moustache launches the Gabriel Knight 3 Cat Moustache puzzle scenario.
Running without flags launches the interactive graphical Tavern Heist simulation at 60 Hz.
entries.why: Continuous integration servers and developer workstations without display servers must be able to run and verify entire multi-scene simulation scenarios with zero GUI dependencies.

entries.title: Standalone Script Runner & Bytecode Packager
entries.summary: CLI subcommands to check, compile, and execute external .bespoke scripts and binary .bspk packages.
entries.synopsis: bespoke run <script.bespoke | game.bspk> [--headless] [--ticks N] | bespoke compile <script> -o <pkg.bspk> | bespoke check <script> | bespoke init <name>
entries.what: Enables narrative designers to author external scenario files on disk, validate syntax with line and column diagnostics, compile them into standalone CRC32-checksummed binary packages (.bspk), and execute them directly without recompiling engine source.
how: bespoke check validates syntax and semantics, reporting file, line, and column error diagnostics on syntax mistakes.
bespoke compile lowers narrative DSL text directly to standalone binary asset packages (.bspk) with magic header BSPB and CRC32 payload verification.
bespoke run executes either text scripts or compiled packages in headless simulation mode or full 60 Hz SDL2 graphical mode.
The asset loader validates header magic, version, payload checksum, and element bounds before allocation, protecting host boundaries from corrupt packages.
bespoke init <name> writes a standalone game project from embedded templates: a build that depends on this engine checkout by relative path, a host, a starter script, and tests (P29-01, D-063).
entries.why: Narrative authors require a decoupled toolchain where content can be written, validated in CI, packaged, and distributed without touching the engine's core Zig code.

entries.title: Peripheral Audio & Procedural Synthesizer
entries.summary: Decoupled audio bridge, procedural chiptune action SFX, and multi-track scene BGM without audio asset files.
entries.synopsis: var bridge = AudioBridge.init(); bridge.enqueue_sfx(.footstep); bridge.set_track(.tavern); bridge.render_samples(&pcm_buffer);
entries.what: A decoupled audio peripheral subsystem synthesizing real-time chiptune action sound effects and 4-channel background musical accompaniments in pure Zig, consuming simulation cues asynchronously with zero WAV/MP3 asset files.
how: AudioBridge consumes discrete audio cues from simulation ticks via an atomic/mutex-guarded ring buffer without blocking the simulation clock.

Procedural ChiptuneSynth generates variable-duty pulse waves, linear triangles, sawteeth, and LCG noise using 32-bit integer phase accumulators and a precomputed 44.1 kHz MIDI table borrowed from Whimsy Machine.

SfxVoice pool synthesizes 10 action sound effects (footsteps, pickups, combining items, horn blasts, splashes, sword clashes, alert stingers, dialogue chirps, clicks, whistles) with attack/decay envelopes and pitch sweeps.

A 4-channel step sequencer synthesizes looping 32-step musical accompaniment across 8 narrative scene themes (.tavern, .cellar, .spitting_contest, .tidewalk, .fencing_yard, .lantern, .courtyard, .bike_shop) with automatic crossfades.
DisplayWindow initializes an SDL2 audio callback feeding 16-bit stereo PCM samples, falling back gracefully to silent offline rendering in headless mode.
entries.why: Narrative immersion requires rich auditory feedback, but BeSpoke's Engine-as-Spine tenet forbids external asset dependencies, blocking audio threads, or non-deterministic simulation execution. Pure procedural integer synthesis guarantees zero asset bloat, instant loading, and 100% headless testability.

entries.title: Persistent Save/Load Storage & Slot Manager
entries.summary: File-backed .sav format with CRC32 integrity, 16x12 RGB332 thumbnails, .bak recovery, and in-engine Save/Load drawer.
entries.synopsis: var sm = try SaveManager.init(allocator, "saves"); _ = try sm.save_slot(1, &world, &spatial, &vm, "Tavern"); _ = try sm.load_slot(1, &world, &spatial, &vm);
entries.what: Provides durable cross-session save/load persistence on disk (.sav), managing 8 numbered save slots plus a dedicated Quick-Save slot with metadata headers, miniature visual frame thumbnails, automatic backup recovery, and an interactive SDL2 Save/Load drawer.
how: write_save_state and read_save_state serialize and restore World relational arenas, SpatialSystem motor agent paths, and VM fiber/interrupt stacks inside a BSAV binary envelope protected by a 32-bit CRC32 checksum.
SaveMetadata embeds playtime, simulation tick, Unix timestamp, fact count, active scene name, actor coordinates, and a 16x12 RGB332 miniature graphical scene thumbnail.

SaveManager preserves any existing valid save as .sav.bak before overwriting; if a primary .sav file fails checksum or header validation on load, it automatically recovers from .sav.bak and repairs the primary file.
DisplayWindow integrates an in-engine Pause & Save/Load Drawer overlay ([P], [F2], [F3]) and 1-key Quick-Save/Quick-Load ([F5], [F9]), rendering each slot's miniature RGB332 thumbnail and metadata.
entries.why: While in-memory arena snapshots enable instant timeline scrubbing during a single session, players and developers also need durable disk saves that preserve mid-walk spatial paths and fiber call stacks while defending against disk truncation or file corruption.

entries.title: Emergent Society Simulation (The Living Village)
entries.summary: Core emergent society mechanic: needs-driven agents, witness detection, rumor propagation, and justice cascades, demonstrated by The Living Village proof.
entries.synopsis: society Hamlet: ... | var soc = try bespoke.society.Society.init(&world, compiled.societies.items[0].config); try soc.step(&world, &spatial, &vm);
entries.what: An engine mechanic for unscripted social simulation (src/society.zig). A script-level society declaration or direct Zig config supplies a list of needs, a roster with data roles (merchant, broadcaster, enforcer) and routines, friendships, and the places the systems use. The Living Village script declares one configuration: 6 villagers across a 6-building settlement.
how: Each need is a property relation with a direction, a per-tick rate, and a seek threshold, met by staying at a place (rest) or by trading with a merchant; past a critical value, a member who cannot pay steals the merchant's goods.
Each tick a member takes the first applicable branch: held, staying, decay, enforcer on duty, start a stay, desperation theft, flight, trade, broadcast, routine.
Aware members near a crime scene while the culprit is there record Witnessed, KnowsRumor, and expiring Grudge facts.
Rumors spread one hop per tick between co-located members who are friends, or when the speaker is a witness or broadcaster, or the listener is the enforcer.

The enforcer issues a warrant with a priority fiber interrupt, pursues, arrests on contact, recovers stolen goods, and escorts the culprit to the holding place. All of this is World facts, so rewind and saves cover it.
CompiledProgram owns society declarations in source order; .bspk format version 4 serializes them and validates their member, waypoint, and entity references.
entries.why: Shows that the flat relational fact store, property auto-overwrite, and priority interrupt spine support unscripted systemic emergence for any cast and setting, with full time-travel scrubbing and disk save compatibility.

entries.title: Script-Declared Dialogue Duels
entries.summary: Challenge/reply contests with learned counters, opponent tiers, fact-guarded candidates, wins, and per-NPC inquiry fatigue.
entries.synopsis: duel RiddleContest: ... | var duel = try bespoke.duel.Duel.init(&world, compiled.duels.items[0].config); try compiled.duels.items[0].apply_tiers(&duel);
entries.what: A reusable dialogue-duel mechanic configured by a script-level duel declaration or direct Zig data. Declarations contain challenge/reply pairs, optional tier variants and opponent assignments, fallback lines, a win threshold, relation vocabulary, and staged inquiry-fatigue moods.
how: Duel.init asserts the immutable Counters and VariantOf knowledge base as World facts; what each fighter heard or mastered, opponent tiers, advantage, wins, inquiry counts, and moods are also facts.
Duel.challenges and Duel.replies submit candidates through VM.prune_dialogue_choices, so the ordinary fact-guarded dialogue query path controls what can be offered.
A duel declaration preserves pair, variant, tier, and fatigue-stage source order. The host applies its tier assignments after Duel.init and may initialize InquiryFatigue from the same declaration.

Fighters learn what they hear (D-078): resolve_round teaches the defender the challenge and the attacker the reply it got back, so a lost round teaches the defender nothing more. Duel.answer gives a host-driven opponent's reply: the countering comeback if it knows it, else the fallback.
Duel.concede lets a fighter give up its turn to attack (D-082): the opponent scores, the fighter's fallback rotation advances, and nobody learns anything.

A fighter with no learned reply is offered one fallback line. The fighter's DuelFumbles count, a fact, picks the line, so successive fumbles rotate through the list and a rewind restores the rotation (D-076).

The Brackwater Barbs proof opens each round as a runtime-generated dialogue set from Duel.replies, resolves the selected reply through Duel.resolve_round, takes turns through the proof's Bout (whoever wins a round attacks next; a master always attacks), moves an attacking opponent to Duel.next_challenge, fires the script's WinsDuel cue for the victory line, and stores the active opponent, barb, and turn as facts so a rewind restores the round (P32-23, D-046).

.bspk format version 4 serializes complete duel declarations; versions 1 through 3 load with an empty declaration table. Version 14 stores up to eight fallback lines; earlier packages hold at most one.
entries.why: Game-facing configuration belongs in distributable .bespoke source. The mechanic remains generic while each game controls its dialogue, tiers, vocabulary, and mood cadence.

entries.title: Showcase Gallery, Script Viewer, and Diagrams
entries.summary: The showcase lists every proof, plays eleven in the viewport, and shows each proof's real script in a viewer that follows the active deck.
entries.synopsis: tools/site_gallery.json -> python3 tools/build_site.py -> SITE_GALLERY region in site/index.html
entries.what: A generated gallery of thirteen proof cards with Play and View script buttons, a line-numbered script viewer under the viewport, and a How It Works section of three inline SVG diagrams.
how: build_site.py reads tools/site_gallery.json and extracts each script from a .bespoke file or a Zig multiline constant (file.zig#CONSTANT).
Scripts are highlighted at build time with the keyword list read from src/compiler/lexer.zig, escaped, and embedded as JSON with </ escaped.
site_simulator.js shows the active deck's script whenever a deck loads, and any proof's script when its View script button is pressed.
build_site.py --check, and deploy_site.py export, treat a changed script or gallery entry as a stale page.
entries.why: Hand-copied snippets had drifted from the proofs. Extracting the scripts at build time keeps the showcase honest, and labelling them as the desktop proofs' source keeps it honest about the browser decks being Zig reconstructions.

entries.title: Showcase Export: Sharing Metadata and an Offline Cache
entries.summary: tools/deploy_site.py turns the self-contained showcase page into a static site with sharing metadata and an offline cache, ready to upload by hand.
entries.synopsis: python3 tools/deploy_site.py export [--site-url https://NAME.neocities.org/]
entries.what: export writes dist/site/index.html and sw.js from site/index.html, which stays unchanged. The maintainer uploads dist/site/ to the host by hand.
how: export refuses a stale page, then adds OpenGraph, Twitter, and theme-colour tags from the page's own title and description, plus canonical and og:url when --site-url is given.
A registration script added before </body> registers sw.js only over http(s), so the file:// page is unaffected.
sw.js names its cache after a hash of the exported page, deletes older caches on activation, and answers from the network first, falling back to the cache offline.
The embedded module is small because the wasm runtime's state is an uninitialised global; node tools/wasm_smoke.js fails any module over 1 MiB.
entries.why: Neocities serves static files and allows no custom headers, so caching and metadata live in the files themselves. Publishing stays a manual step the maintainer takes (D-074), so the repository holds no host credentials.

entries.title: WebAssembly (wasm32-freestanding) Target & Browser Runtime
entries.summary: Zero-dependency wasm32-freestanding RGBA8888 runtime with a browser event bridge; games supply its scenes as decks.
entries.synopsis: zig build wasm wasm-proofs | wasm_init(deck); wasm_step_tick(); wasm_render_frame(); wasm_on_pointer_down(x, y);
entries.what: Compiles the BeSpoke Engine simulation spine to a zero-dependency wasm32-freestanding WebAssembly module with a 640x360 RGBA8888 software framebuffer and a browser mouse/keyboard/touch event bridge. What is on stage comes from a deck table the host compiles in: the engine's own module has one neutral demo deck, and bespoke-proofs.wasm carries seven proof decks.
how: WasmCanvas renders rooms, topological waypoint edges, interactive hotspots, actor tokens, bitmap font strings, a timeline scrubber bar, and the 5-verb bar into a contiguous 640x360x4 RGBA8888 byte buffer in linear memory.

WasmRuntime manages World, SpatialSystem, BytecodeChunk, VM, and a 32-slot ring buffer of binary World snapshots inside a 2 MiB FixedBufferAllocator. Each Deck supplies load, after-tick, and catalyst callbacks, and wasm.export_runtime(decks) emits the C-ABI exports (wasm_init, wasm_step_tick, wasm_framebuffer_ptr, wasm_scrub_to_tick) for a build's decks.

dispatch_event normalizes browser pointer_down, pointer_move, right_click, key_down, and touch events into BeSpoke walk_to motor intents, verb selection, hotspot inspection, catalyst triggers, and timeline scrubbing.

The engine synthesizer plays in the browser (D-071): the runtime's AudioBridge renders the script's scores or a deck's soundtrack, and the page pulls stereo samples with wasm_audio_render into Web Audio. A deck can own a TemporalHypervisor whose live branch the VM, story, and inspector follow and the timeline records; draft decks play notes on C to B.

I opens the state inspector over the stage (D-070): the desktop State tab's ego graph, values, dialogue branches, and next expirations, from the same capture and state_graph layout, with the clock paused and the desktop's keys sent as DOM key codes.

Script decks (wasm.script_deck_with) compile a game's or a proof's script in the browser, start it with host.start_script, and tick through host.tick. Verbs on people and props fire LooksAt, TalksTo, Takes, or Uses for the deck's player; the number keys answer an open dialogue; the stage draws only the current room, fitted to the canvas (D-066, D-069).

The standalone showcase website (site/index.html) embeds bespoke-proofs.wasm via tools/build_site.py to provide a live interactive simulation viewport. tools/wasm_smoke.js exercises both modules in Node.
entries.why: Targeting wasm32-freestanding with an in-memory RGBA8888 framebuffer preserves BeSpoke's zero-external-dependency guarantee (no Emscripten or SDL2 required). Decks keep game content out of the engine module (D-042), and the interactive simulator lives on the public showcase site rather than inside the reference manual (D-047).

sections.title: Developer Guide & Engineering Standards
sections.description: Contribution standards, verification hierarchies, architectural decision records, and documentation tooling.

entries.title: Test Verification Hierarchy
entries.summary: Multi-tiered automated test suite verifying compiler, VM, spatial system, renderer, and scenarios.
entries.synopsis: zig test -lc -lSDL2 src/root.zig && zig build test && python3 tools/check_docs.py
entries.what: Enforces code correctness across all engine modules via fast, unit-level Zig test blocks, build-system tests, headless simulations, and documentation consistency checks.
how: zig test -lc -lSDL2 src/root.zig runs 95 core compiler, VM, world, spatial, audio, save, village, and wasm tests.
zig test -lc -lSDL2 src/display.zig runs 61 display bridge, font, and renderer tests.
zig test src/wasm.zig && zig build wasm verifies the freestanding WebAssembly runtime and browser event bridge.
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v runs 29 documentation manual tests.
python3 tools/check_docs.py validates cross-references, decision numbers, and session logs.
python3 tools/manual.py check scheme/bespoke.manual.json --check-evidence --root . verifies manual integrity.
entries.why: Unit tests, proof transcripts compared with goldens, render and audio hashes, and documentation checks catch changes to grammar, opcodes, or layout that alter simulation behaviour.

entries.title: Architectural Decision Records (D-NNN)
entries.summary: Append-only architectural decision log in docs/DECISIONS.md recording rationale and alternatives.
entries.synopsis:
## D-NNN Title (YYYY-MM-DD, status: accepted)
Context: ...
Decision: ...
Alternatives: ...
Consequences: ...
entries.what: Maintains an immutable record of technical and design choices, documenting the context, trade-offs, evaluated alternatives, and consequences for every significant architectural evolution.
how: Decisions are assigned monotonically increasing IDs (D-001 through D-031).
Each decision details Context, Decision, Alternatives Considered, and Consequences.
Open architectural questions are logged in the same document with permanent Q-NNN IDs until answered.
entries.why: Without written decision records, future maintainers and AI agents revisit already-rejected trade-offs or accidentally undo foundational constraints (such as zero-dependency or tick determinism).

entries.title: The 3x What/How/Why Documentation Contract
entries.summary: Every documented component answers What it does, How it works, and Why, backed by explicit evidence.
entries.synopsis: python3 tools/manual.py build scheme/bespoke.manual.json --output docs/manual.html
entries.what: Governs all technical documentation using the 3x documentation scheme: every subject answers What, How, and Why, and cites verifiable code and decision evidence.
how: Source is defined in JSON validated against scheme/manual.schema.json.
tools/manual.py builds a portable, zero-dependency HTML manual with interactive search and navigation.
why_basis tracks provenance: recorded, observed, inferred, or external.
tools/manual.py check --check-evidence verifies that every cited file, decision, and test exists in the repository.
entries.why: Traditional freeform documentation frequently omits rationale, goes stale, or drifts from code reality. The 3x contract gives human developers and coding agents the reason behind each component and the code that backs it.
